title: V. Not You, Not You!
paragraphs: On his way to Ivan, he had to pass the house where Katerina Ivanovna lived. Light showed in the windows. He stopped suddenly and decided to go in. He hadn't seen Katerina Ivanovna in more than a week. But now it struck him that Ivan might be with her, especially on the eve of this terrible day. He rang, climbed the staircase, dimly lit by a Chinese lantern, and saw a man coming down; as they met, he recognized his brother. So Ivan was just now coming from Katerina Ivanovna's.
"Ah, it's only you," Ivan said dryly. "Well, good-bye! You're going up to her?"
"Yes."
"I don't advise it; she's upset, and you'll only upset her more."
A door flew open above them at once, and a voice cried out:
"No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, have you come from him?"
"Yes, I've just been with him."
"Did he send me any message? Come up, Alyosha—and you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you have to come back, you have to. Do you hear?"
There was such a commanding note in Katya's voice that Ivan, after a moment's hesitation, made up his mind to go back up with Alyosha.
"She was listening at the door," he muttered angrily to himself, but Alyosha caught it.
"Forgive me for keeping my coat on," Ivan said, walking into the drawing room. "I won't sit down. I won't stay more than a minute."

"Sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch," Katerina Ivanovna said, though she herself remained standing. She'd changed very little in this time, but there was an ominous gleam in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered afterward that she'd struck him as especially beautiful in that moment.
"What did he ask you to tell me?"

"Just one thing," Alyosha said, looking her straight in the face, "that you'd spare yourself, and say nothing at the trial about what"—he faltered a little—"...passed between you...when you first met...in that town."

"Ah! That I bowed down to the ground for that money!" She broke into a bitter laugh. "So, is he afraid for me, or for himself? He's asking me to spare—whom? Him, or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!"
Alyosha watched her closely, trying to understand her.
"Both you and him," he answered softly.
"I'm glad to hear it," she snapped, with sudden malice, and then abruptly blushed.
"You don't know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch," she said, almost threateningly. "And I don't know myself yet, either. Maybe after my testimony tomorrow you'll want to trample me underfoot."
"You'll give your testimony honorably," Alyosha said. "That's all that's needed."

"Women are often dishonorable," she snarled. "Only an hour ago I was thinking I couldn't bear to touch that monster...as if he were some reptile...but no, he's still a human being to me! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?" she cried out suddenly, almost hysterically, turning sharply to Ivan. Alyosha realized at once that she'd asked Ivan that question before—maybe only a moment before he'd arrived, and not for the first time, but the hundredth—and that it had ended in a quarrel between them.

"I've been to see Smerdyakov.... It was you, you who convinced me he murdered his father. You're the only one I believed!" she went on, still addressing Ivan. He gave her a strained sort of smile. Alyosha started at her tone. He hadn't suspected such intimacy between them.
"Well, that's enough, anyway," Ivan cut the conversation short. "I'm going. I'll come tomorrow." And turning at once, he walked out of the room and went straight downstairs.
With a commanding gesture, Katerina Ivanovna seized Alyosha by both hands.

"Go after him! Catch up with him! Don't leave him alone for a minute!" she said in a hurried whisper. "He's out of his mind! Don't you know he's out of his mind? He's got a fever, a nervous fever. The doctor told me so. Go, run after him...."
Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not fifty paces ahead of him.
"What do you want?" he turned sharply on Alyosha when he saw him running after him. "She told you to catch me up, because I'm out of my mind. I know it all by heart," he added irritably.
"She's mistaken, of course, but she's right that you're ill," Alyosha said. "I was looking at your face just now. You look very ill, Ivan."
Ivan kept walking without stopping. Alyosha followed him.
"And do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how people actually go out of their minds?" Ivan asked, his voice suddenly calm, with no trace of irritation left in it, just a note of plain curiosity.
"No, I don't. I suppose there are all kinds of madness."
"And can a person tell that they're going mad themselves?"
"I'd imagine one can't see oneself clearly in circumstances like that," Alyosha answered, surprised.
Ivan paused for half a minute.
"If you want to talk to me, please change the subject," he said suddenly.

"Oh, while I think of it, I have a letter for you," Alyosha said timidly, and took Lise's note from his pocket, holding it out to Ivan. They were standing right under a streetlamp. Ivan recognized the handwriting at once.
"Ah, from that little demon!" he laughed maliciously, and without opening the envelope, tore it to pieces and tossed them into the air. The wind scattered the scraps.
"She's not even sixteen yet, I believe, and already throwing herself at people," he said contemptuously, striding on down the street again.
"What do you mean, throwing herself at people?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"The way loose women throw themselves at people, of course."

"How can you say that, Ivan, how can you?" Alyosha cried, warmly, his voice pained. "She's a child; you're insulting a child! She's ill, badly ill. She might be on the verge of madness herself.... I'd hoped to hear something from you...something that would save her."
"You won't hear anything from me. If she's a child, I'm not her nursemaid. Be quiet, Alexey. Don't go on about her. I'm not even thinking about it."
They fell silent again for a moment.
"She'll spend all night now praying to the Mother of God, asking how to act tomorrow at the trial," he said, sharp and angry again.
"You...you mean Katerina Ivanovna?"

"Yes. Whether to save Mitya or ruin him. She'll pray for light from above. She can't make up her own mind, you see. She hasn't had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nursemaid too. She wants me to sing her lullabies."
"Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother," Alyosha said sadly.
"Maybe; but I'm not especially keen on her."
"She's suffering. Then why do you...sometimes say things to her that give her hope?" Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. "I know you've given her hope. Forgive me for saying this to you," he added.

"I can't do the right thing by her—break it off completely and tell her so outright," Ivan said irritably. "I have to wait until sentence is passed on the murderer. If I break with her now, she'll take revenge on me by destroying that scoundrel tomorrow at the trial, because she hates him, and she knows she hates him. It's all lies—lie upon lie! As long as I don't break with her, she keeps hoping, and she won't destroy that monster, knowing how much I want to see him get off. If only that damned verdict would come already!"
The words "murderer" and "monster" echoed painfully in Alyosha's heart.
"But how could she ruin Mitya?" he asked, turning Ivan's words over. "What evidence could she give that would ruin him?"
"You don't know that yet. She's got a document in her hands, in Mitya's own handwriting, that proves beyond doubt that he murdered Fyodor Pavlovitch."
"That's impossible!" Alyosha cried.
"Why is it impossible? I've read it myself."
"There can't be a document like that!" Alyosha repeated fiercely. "There can't be, because he's not the murderer. It wasn't him who killed father, not him!"
Ivan stopped short.
"Then who's the murderer, according to you?" he asked, with a show of coldness. There was even something supercilious in his tone.
"You know who," Alyosha said, in a low, piercing voice.
"Who? You mean that myth about the crazy idiot, the epileptic—Smerdyakov?"
Alyosha suddenly felt himself trembling all over.
"You know who," broke helplessly from him. He could hardly breathe.
"Who? Who?" Ivan cried, almost savagely. All his restraint vanished in an instant.
"I know only one thing," Alyosha went on, still nearly in a whisper, "it wasn't you who killed father."
"'Not you'! What do you mean, 'not you'?" Ivan was thunderstruck.
"It was not you who killed father, not you!" Alyosha repeated firmly.
The silence lasted half a minute.
"I know I didn't. Are you raving?" Ivan said, with a pale, twisted smile. His eyes were fixed on Alyosha. They were standing again under a streetlamp.
"No, Ivan. You've told yourself, several times, that you're the murderer."
"When did I say that? I was in Moscow.... When have I ever said that?" Ivan faltered helplessly.

"You've said it to yourself many times, when you've been alone these last two terrible months," Alyosha went on, softly and distinctly, as before. Yet he was speaking now, it seemed, not on his own behalf, not by his own will, but under some command he couldn't resist. "You've accused yourself, and confessed to yourself, that you're the murderer and no one else. But you didn't do it: you're mistaken: you're not the murderer. Do you hear? It was not you! God has sent me to tell you so."

They were both silent. The silence stretched out a whole long minute. They stood still, staring into each other's eyes. Both were pale. Suddenly Ivan began trembling all over, and clutched Alyosha's shoulder.
"You've been in my room!" he whispered hoarsely. "You've been there at night, when he came.... Confess...have you seen him, have you seen him?"
"Who do you mean—Mitya?" Alyosha asked, bewildered.
"Not him, damn the monster!" Ivan shouted, in a frenzy. "Do you know that he visits me? How did you find out? Speak!"
"Who is he? I don't know who you're talking about," Alyosha faltered, starting to feel alarmed.
"Yes, you do know...or how could you—? It's impossible that you don't know."
He suddenly seemed to catch himself. He stood still and appeared to think it over. A strange grin twisted his lips.

"Brother," Alyosha began again, in a shaking voice, "I've said this to you because you'll believe my word—I know that. I'm telling you once and for all, it's not you. Do you hear, once and for all! God put it in my heart to say this to you, even if it means you'll hate me from this hour on."
But by now Ivan seemed to have regained his self-control.

"Alexey Fyodorovitch," he said, with a cold smile, "I can't stand prophets and epileptics—messengers from God especially—and you know that perfectly well. I'm breaking off all relations with you as of this moment, probably for good. I ask you to leave me here at this corner. It's the way to your lodgings too, anyway. And you'd do especially well not to come see me today! Do you hear?"
He turned and walked on with a firm step, without looking back.
"Brother," Alyosha called after him, "if anything happens to you today, come to me before anyone else!"

But Ivan didn't answer. Alyosha stood under the streetlamp at the crossroads until Ivan had vanished into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan were living in lodgings; neither was willing to live in Fyodor Pavlovitch's empty house. Alyosha had a furnished room in the home of some working people. Ivan lived some distance away from him. He'd taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house belonging to a well-to-do lady, the widow of an official. But his only attendant was a deaf, rheumatic old woman who went to bed at six every evening and got up at six in the morning. Ivan had grown remarkably indifferent to his own comfort of late, and very fond of being alone. He did everything for himself in the one room he lived in, and rarely set foot in any of the other rooms of his lodgings.

He reached the gate of the house and had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He felt himself trembling all over with anger. Suddenly he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse, and walked off rapidly in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a small, leaning wooden house, almost a hut, where Marya Kondratyevna now lodged—the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch's kitchen for soup, and to whom Smerdyakov had once sung songs and played the guitar. She'd sold their little house and was now living here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill—nearly dying—had been staying with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch's death. It was to him Ivan was going now, drawn by a sudden and irresistible urge.
